```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

```text

- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust

```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust

AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```

---

Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:

---

Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

---
name: typst
description: "Typst document creation and package development. Use when: (1) Working with .typ files, (2) User mentions typst, typst.toml, or typst-cli, (3) Creating or using Typst packages, (4) Developing document templates, (5) Converting Markdown/LaTeX to Typst"
---

# Typst

Typst is a modern typesetting system designed as an alternative to LaTeX. It offers a simpler syntax, faster compilation, and programmatic document creation.

## Agent Patterns

### Detection

```bash
typst --version  # Check if installed
```

### Verify Compilation

Agents cannot preview PDFs. Verify success via exit code:

```bash
typst compile document.typ && echo "Success" || echo "Failed"
```

For text-level verification, see [debug.md](debug.md) (`pdftotext` workflow).

### Common Errors

| Error                                  | Cause                | Fix                                        |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| "unknown variable"                     | Undefined identifier | Check spelling, ensure `#let` before use   |
| "expected X, found Y"                  | Type mismatch        | Check function signature in docs           |
| "file not found"                       | Bad import path      | Paths resolve relative to the current file |
| "unknown font"                         | Font not installed   | Use system fonts or web-safe alternatives  |
| "maximum function call depth exceeded" | Deep recursion       | Limit recursion, use iteration instead     |

### Minimal Document

```typst
#set page(paper: "a4", margin: 2cm)
#set text(size: 11pt)

= Title

Content goes here.
```

## Quick Reference

| Task                                            | Reference                      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Language basics (types, functions, operators)   | [basics.md](basics.md)         |
| State, context, query, XML parsing              | [advanced.md](advanced.md)     |
| Templates, styling, set/show rules              | [template.md](template.md)     |
| Package development, publishing                 | [package.md](package.md)       |
| Converting from Markdown/LaTeX                  | [conversion.md](conversion.md) |
| Debugging techniques (pdftotext, repr, measure) | [debug.md](debug.md)           |
| Performance profiling (timings, hotspots)       | [perf.md](perf.md)             |

## When to Use Each Reference

### basics.md

**Read first** for any Typst work. Complete language reference:

- Markup vs code mode switching
- **Imports and path resolution** (relative, root-relative, `--root`)
- All data types and their operations (string, array, dict)
- Regex pattern matching
- Functions, control flow, operators
- Common pitfalls (closure mutability, none returns)

### advanced.md

For cross-document features and complex patterns:

- State management (`state()`, `context`)
- Query system (`query()`, metadata, labels)
- XML parsing
- Working around closure limitations
- Performance optimization

### template.md

For document templates and styling:

- Set rules (defaults) and show rules (transformations)
- Page layout, headers, footers
- Counters and numbering
- Heading and figure customization

### package.md

For creating reusable Typst packages:

- `typst.toml` manifest format
- Module organization and imports
- API design patterns
- Publishing to Typst Universe

### conversion.md

For converting existing documents to Typst:

- Syntax mapping tables (Markdown/LaTeX → Typst)
- Math formula conversion
- Escaping rules
- Pandoc integration

### debug.md

For debugging Typst documents (especially for agents):

- `pdftotext` for text content verification
- `repr()` for inspecting complex objects
- `measure()` + `place()` for layout debugging
- State and query debugging patterns

### perf.md

For performance profiling and timing analysis:

- `--timings` JSON trace output
- Aggregating hotspots from trace events
- Viewing traces in Chrome/Perfetto

## Compilation

```bash
# Compile once
typst compile document.typ

# Watch mode (recompile on changes)
typst watch document.typ

# Specify output file
typst compile document.typ output.pdf

# Set project root (for multi-file projects)
# Root controls where "/path" resolves and security boundary
typst compile src/main.typ --root .
```

**When to use `--root`**: If your document imports files using `/`-prefixed paths (e.g., `#import "/lib/utils.typ"`), set `--root` to the directory those paths should resolve from. See [basics.md](basics.md) for path resolution rules.

## Common Packages

| Package              | Purpose                                        |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `@preview/codly`     | Code block formatting with syntax highlighting |
| `@preview/ctheorems` | Theorem environments                           |
| `@preview/mitex`     | LaTeX math rendering                           |
| `@preview/cuti`      | CJK typography utilities                       |
| `@preview/citegeist` | BibTeX parsing                                 |

Import packages (check https://typst.app/universe for latest versions):

```typst
#import "@preview/codly:1.3.0": *
```

## Examples

The `examples/` directory contains runnable examples:

| Example                                             | Description                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| [basic-document.typ](examples/basic-document.typ)   | Complete beginner document with all common elements  |
| [template-report.typ](examples/template-report.typ) | Reusable template with headers, counters, note boxes |
| [package-example/](examples/package-example/)       | Minimal publishable package with submodules          |

## Dependencies

- **typst CLI**: Install from https://typst.app or via package manager
  - macOS: `brew install typst`
  - Linux: `cargo install typst-cli`
  - Windows: `winget install typst`

# SYSTEM INSTRUCTION: Presentation Generation & Planning Standard

You are an expert technical communicator. Your task is to generate highly precise Typst slide decks and their prerequisite "Slide Plans" based on repository artifacts (specs, code, reports).

---

## 🛠️ Section 1: The Workflow
You must work in two distinct phases. Do not build the deck until the plan is finalized.

### Phase 1: Write the Slide Plan (`presentation/YYYY-MM-DD/<slug>/plan.md`)
- Every slide deck keeps its plan beside the slide source. Every slide element must be justified in that local `plan.md` before it reaches code.
- Spawn subagents to follow the planned change in implementing hte actual slide deck.

### Phase 2: Implementation & Compilation (`presentation/YYYY-MM-DD/<slug>/`)
1. **File Hygiene:** Keep `plan.md`, one primary `.typ` entry file, and deck-local assets in the same dated topic folder. Use `deck.typ` as the primary entry point unless a deck already has an established name.
2. **Touying-native Typst slides:** Build decks on the shared `presentation/template.typ` Touying setup. Use Touying/Typst-native slide structure (`#show: deck.with(...)`, `#slide[...]`) and native Typst constructs for layout and content. Do not invent custom slide frameworks, manual page counters, or custom numbered-list helpers; use native `+`/`-` lists and scoped `#set enum(...)` / `#set list(...)` styling when accents are needed.
3. **Preview Compilation:** During iteration, compile pages to PNG for visual inspection under `assets/previews/` using:
   `typst compile --format png --ppi 288 --root presentation presentation/YYYY-MM-DD/<slug>/deck.typ presentation/YYYY-MM-DD/<slug>/assets/previews/preview-slide-{p}.png`
4. **Final Delivery:** Export to PDF only at the final stage or for text-extraction/archival checks.

---

## ❌ Anti-Patterns to Avoid
* Creating undated, floating presentation directories.
* Writing slide plans outside the deck folder, or with vague placeholders like "Slide 4: Results" without specifying exact numbers and modules.
* Adding elements during Typst coding that were never mapped out in the plan.
* Sacrificing 16:9 layout readability for dense text panels.

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.

- invalid wire format

Job:

  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Balance scale:

The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

<attachment>
You’re right. The prompt should specify the deck architecture: each slide’s teaching job, not just facts to include.

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:

- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:

- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```
