```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

- retry/drop state

- This made suspension explicit.

`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Title:

Content:
Mention evidence:

- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

    + 'static;

- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Content:

- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:

---

Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Content:
Explain:

- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Visual:

`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field

- invalid wire format

Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:

- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,

- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```
</attachment> Create a typst slide presentation based on this; you should try to use existing typst package for making more beautiful slide (such as zebraw or other visualization packages);

- whether tag was already written

- whether payload copy is pending

- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:

`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:

---

Explain the final outer API.

Title:

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

State the key nuance clearly.

Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Explain the first design trap.

- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical

Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:

- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.

```text
Create a technical teaching slide deck about the evolution from sync Tonic encode to async DSA-backed Prost encode.

Audience:
Systems/Rust researchers familiar with async Rust, Tonic/gRPC, Prost, and accelerators, but not familiar with this repo’s encode redesign.

Deck goal:
Teach that async encode was an ownership/state-machine redesign, not a mechanical `async fn` rewrite. The deck must make the intermediate poll-based codec design explicit, then show why poll encode moved down into Prost while the Tonic boundary ended up using owned futures.

Core thesis:
“Poll encode was not removed; it migrated from the Tonic codec boundary into the Prost field-level state machine.”

Deck structure:

Slide 1 — Thesis / mental model
Job:
Establish the central lesson before details.

Title:
“Async Encode Was an Ownership Redesign”

Content:
- Old instinct: “make `encode()` async”
- Actual solution: owned resumable state + stable buffers + exact protobuf resume points
- One-line arc:
  `sync encode → async experiments → poll codec API → owned futures at Tonic boundary → poll Prost field engine`

Visual:
A simple horizontal evolution arrow with the final thesis highlighted.

Speaker message:
This was not about sprinkling async. It was about deciding who owns state while encoding is suspended.

---

Slide 2 — Baseline: sync encode was simple because nothing suspended
Job:
Ground the audience in the original design and why it worked.

Title:
“Sync Encode: Borrow, Write, Return”

Content:
Show the old shape conceptually:

```rust
fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Explain:
- Encoder borrows output buffer.
- CPU writes payload immediately.
- No state survives the call.
- gRPC framing can happen around a completed buffer.

Visual:
Small flow:
`message → encoder → borrowed EncodeBuf → completed bytes`

Speaker message:
The sync design is elegant because all lifetimes are stack-local.

---

Slide 3 — Why naive async encode fails
Job:
Explain the first design trap.

Title:
“Why `async fn encode(&mut self, &mut buf)` Is the Wrong Shape”

Content:
Show tempting shape:

```rust
async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf) -> Result<()>
```

Then show why it breaks:
- Future would borrow encoder and destination across `Pending`.
- Tonic body driver needs an in-flight operation it can store and poll.
- DSA may retain raw source/destination pointers after returning `Pending`.
- `Send + 'static` pushes against borrowed state.

Visual:
A warning diagram:
`borrowed &mut buffer` crosses a red `Pending` boundary.

Speaker message:
The problem is not syntax; it is that suspension turns temporary borrows into long-lived state.

---

Slide 4 — Historical turning point: codec-level poll encode
Job:
Make the intermediate design explicit, because this is easy to lose in the story.

Title:
“Middle Design: Poll-Based Codec Encode”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `0f4d329 Use poll-based codec API`

Explain:
- The project did try a poll-based codec boundary.
- This made suspension explicit.
- It let the driver ask: “are encoded bytes ready yet?”
- But it still left pressure around where state lives and how much of Tonic should know about encode internals.

Visual:
A poll loop:
`poll_encode(cx) -> Pending`
`poll_encode(cx) -> Ready(buffer)`

Speaker message:
Poll encode existed first at the Tonic codec boundary. That design was real, not imaginary.

---

Slide 5 — Why ownership moved into the encoder
Job:
Teach the first major correction after poll-based experiments.

Title:
“Suspension Requires Encoder-Owned State”

Content:
Mention evidence:
- `a415231 Make async encode state encoder-owned`
- `617cd50 Split encoder async state`

Explain:
State that may survive `Pending` must be owned:
- message/item
- destination buffer
- protobuf field position
- pending payload copy
- DSA descriptor/completion
- retry/drop state

Visual:
Before/after:
Before:
`driver owns too much temporary state`
After:
`encoder future owns resumable encode state`

Speaker message:
Once encoding can suspend, “where does the state live?” becomes the API design question.

---

Slide 6 — Current Tonic boundary: owned future
Job:
Explain the final outer API.

Title:
“Final Tonic Boundary: Encode Returns an Owned Future”

Content:
Show current conceptual shape:

```rust
type Encode: Future<Output = Result<EncodeBuffer, Error>>
    + Send
    + 'static;

fn encode(
    self: Pin<&mut Self>,
    item: Item,
    dst: EncodeBuffer,
) -> Result<Self::Encode>;
```

Explain:
- `EncodeBuffer` is owned by the encode future.
- Tonic stores `in_flight: Option<T::Encode>`.
- Sync encoders return ready futures.
- Tonic regains the buffer only when encode completes.

Visual:
`Tonic driver → starts future → polls future → receives EncodeBuffer`

Speaker message:
The Tonic boundary became future-based because that is the cleanest unit for the body driver to store and poll.

---

Slide 7 — Tonic still owns gRPC framing
Job:
Prevent misunderstanding that the encoder owns the whole wire format.

Title:
“Tonic Still Finalizes the Frame”

Content:
Explain the driver responsibilities:
- reserve 5-byte gRPC header before encode
- poll in-flight encode
- regain returned `EncodeBuffer`
- apply compression if needed
- enforce max message size
- write final gRPC length header
- yield bytes downstream

Visual:
Pipeline:
`reserve header → async encode body → compression/size check → write header → yield frame`

Speaker message:
Async encode produces the message body; Tonic still owns protocol framing.

---

Slide 8 — Poll encode did not disappear; it moved down into Prost
Job:
State the key nuance clearly.

Title:
“Poll Encode Migrated Down a Layer”

Content:
Show contrast:

Outer Tonic boundary:

```rust
encode(...) -> Future<Output = EncodeBuffer>
```

Inner Prost engine:

```rust
Message::poll_encode_raw(...)
AsyncEncodeTarget
PollEncodeState
```

Explain:
- Tonic wants one owned async operation.
- Prost needs exact field-level resume points.
- Therefore poll remains the right abstraction inside protobuf encoding.

Visual:
Layer diagram:

```text
Tonic body driver
  └─ owned encode future
       └─ Prost poll_encode_raw state machine
            └─ DSA/CPU payload target
```

Speaker message:
Poll encode was not rejected. It was moved to the layer where fine-grained resume state actually belongs.

---

Slide 9 — Prost challenge: exact resume without byte corruption
Job:
Teach why protobuf makes async encoding hard.

Title:
“Protobuf Resume State Must Be Exact”

Content:
Explain that after `Pending`, the encoder must know:
- which field it was encoding
- which repeated/map index
- whether tag was already written
- whether length prefix was already written
- whether payload copy is pending
- whether nested message/oneof state is active

Failure modes:
- duplicate tag
- duplicate length prefix
- skipped field
- payload written at wrong offset
- invalid wire format

Visual:
A protobuf field split into phases:
`tag → length → payload`
with `Pending` only allowed after state records the completed phases.

Speaker message:
Async protobuf encoding is a resumable compiler for wire-format bytes.

---

Slide 10 — DSA challenge: hardware makes ownership physical
Job:
Explain why accelerator support is stricter than ordinary async I/O.

Title:
“DSA Turns Lifetimes Into Hardware Safety”

Content:
Explain DSA-specific constraints:
- source pointer must remain valid
- destination pointer must remain stable
- `BytesMut` must not reallocate while DMA owns destination
- descriptor/completion must stay alive
- page-fault retry may be needed
- drop/cancel must drain in-flight work before freeing memory

Visual:
DMA diagram:
`owned message memory → DSA descriptor → stable EncodeBuffer storage`

Speaker message:
With hardware DMA, Rust ownership mistakes become memory corruption risks, not just type errors.

---

Slide 11 — Performance lesson: remove staged copies, but don’t promise universal wins
Job:
Connect design to measurement without overclaiming.

Title:
“Async DSA Enables Measurement, Not Guaranteed Speedup”

Content:
Explain:
- Direct async DSA into final encode storage removes staged-copy overhead.
- This materially changed benchmark regimes.
- Wins were workload-dependent.
- The cost model includes:
  - submission overhead
  - polling/wakeup
  - state machine overhead
  - page-fault/retry
  - avoided CPU copy size

Visual:
Balance scale:
`avoided CPU copy` vs `DSA async overhead`

Speaker message:
The design makes hardware useful when payload and regime justify it; it does not make every encode faster.

---

Slide 12 — Final takeaway
Job:
Leave audience with the design rule they can reuse.

Title:
“Reusable Design Rule”

Content:
Main statement:

```text
If an operation can suspend, anything needed after suspension
must be owned by the suspended operation.
```

Apply it here:
- Tonic owns stream/framing state.
- Encode future owns message + buffer + hardware state.
- Prost poll state owns exact wire-format resume position.
- CPU encode remains a ready future.

Final emphasized sentence:
“Async encode is owned resumable state plus exact protocol resume points.”

Visual:
Three ownership boxes:
`Tonic framing`
`Encode future`
`Prost field state`

Speaker message:
The final architecture works because each layer owns the state at its own granularity.
```
